evidence: Word-by-word comparison, on the current files (CONTEXT.txt now has the curly "Let’s" in the next paragraph; DRAFT.txt and SOURCE.txt are unchanged). SOURCE (the approved working-copy line it replaces): "A script you could use for anxiety is:". DRAFT: "Here is a little script you could use:". Kept: "script you could use", so the offer stays an offer ("could", the reader is the one who uses it) and the colon still hands over the script that follows. Dropped: "for anxiety". the_change says the heading carries it, and it does: CONTEXT.txt opens with the heading "Anxiety script" on the line directly above the draft, so nothing of the source's meaning is lost; the change claims to put nothing back, so nothing is owed. Added: "Here is" (a pointing frame, no claim) and "a little" (an informal size word, not a claim, condition, person or number; the script that follows is three short paragraphs, so it is not untrue, and it does not change the strength of the offer or who does what). The draft is exactly Emulate's phrase named in the_change; no other words differ. Read in context, the heading, the lead-in and the script after it read in order and right. Tell rows, judged on the literal draft in its section. T19 is PRESENT: the sentence's whole job is to announce the script that comes next. I judge it justified: it is the same job his approved line did, so the change adds no announcement he had not approved; the colon frames a block of first-person script lines that a reader would otherwise take for his own narration; and it carries the "could" (a suggestion, not an order). The writer's ledger marks T19 ABSENT ("does not announce what comes next"), which is not accurate on a literal reading, but it makes no difference to the verdict. T11 considered: without "for anxiety" the lead-in could be reused above any script, but it introduces one block, it does not bridge two document parts, and the topic sits in the heading directly above; not present. T26 considered: "little" in "a little script" and in the script's "little one", and "script" in heading and lead-in; "little" is an ordinary word, and the heading-plus-lead-in "script" is the same as in the source; not present. T22 not present (a one-line offer, no reassurance); T25 not present (the colon introduces a real quoted script); T24 not present ("Here is" hands over an object, it manufactures no suspense); C01 to C04 absent (no naming of the inner child, no referent, no first-person fact, no named entity); every other row (T01 to T10, T12 to T18, T20, T21, T23, T27 to T29) absent in a one-line lead-in. Linter findings. B7 short landing at paragraph end ("Here is a little script you could use:"): not a real problem; it is a lead-in that ends on a colon with the script in the next paragraphs, not a closer, exactly as the old line was; accepted. D9 follows the source order (1/1, agreement 1.00): a single re-worded line has nothing to reorder, and T13 and T09 do not apply to a one-line lead-in; accepted. E36/E41 heavy second person (12.5 "you" per 100 words): an artifact of counting one "you" in eight words; the source line has the same one "you" in eight words ("you could use"), so the draft adds no second person; accepted. Side note: the writer's ledger lines for T14 and T15 ("puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped") do not fit this card, since nothing is put back; that is boilerplate, not a draft problem.
